description.value:
The chart's axes define the visual structure of the data and can be customized to match different visualization needs. Configuration options include split lines, label visibility and formatting, axis positioning, data range constraints, and support for multiple axes. For a full reference of all available options see the ECharts documentation for [xAxis](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#xAxis) and [yAxis](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#yAxis). **Split lines** Split lines help users relate data points to their corresponding axis values and make values easier to compare across the chart.
  • Use split lines on value axes when comparing or estimating values is important.
  • Keep split lines subtle so they provide visual guidance without competing with the data.
  • Avoid unnecessary split lines on category axes when categories are already clearly separated and labeled.
  • Consider hiding split lines for simple charts where they do not add meaningful orientation.
The default is, that both axes lines as well as the split lines are hidden.
If you want to display both axes lines and split lines, use the handle method `axesShowSplitLines()`.
To show only horizontal split lines, use the handle method `axesShowYSplitLines()`.
To show only vertical split lines, use the handle method `axesShowXSplitLines()`.
If you want to hide the axis labels, use the handle method `axesHideLabels()`.
To show axes split lines but hide axis labels, combine `axesShowSplitLines()` and `axesHideLabels()`.

title.value: Visible Axes Lines with Hidden Values

description.value: To add icons to axis labels, use the handle methods `axesAddXLabelIcons()` and `axesAddYLabelIcons()`.
The default position of the y-axis is left and for the x-axis is bottom. The axes can be positioned at the top, bottom, left or right of the chart by using the `position` option.
The default min and max values of the axes are calculated automatically based on the data. The min and max values can be set manually by using the `min` and `max` options for the axes.

To add multiple y-axes to the chart, define an array of y-axis configurations under the `yAxis` option. Shared y-axes are positioned on the left side by default, and you can specify the position for each axis individually.

This chart compares two metrics (temperature, precipitation) for two countries (Germany, France) using a single shared axis approach, encoded through visual channels that do not depend on color perception at all:

 **1. Line style and marker shape = country** 
Germany is drawn with solid lines and filled square/circle markers; France is drawn with dotted lines. This distinction is fully readable in grayscale or black-and-white print, since it relies on stroke pattern and shape rather than hue. 

**2. Legend labels = explicit redundant encoding**
Rather than expecting the reader to decode line style or marker shape from a key, each legend entry spells out both dimensions in text: "Temperature Germany", "Preciptation France". This turns the legend itself into a self-sufficient lookup table, so no single visual channel has to carry the full weight of disambiguation.

Color is still used in this chart (blue/green) to make the two metrics faster to tell apart on screen, but it is treated as a supporting cue only and never as the sole means of distinguishing a series. Every distinction the chart makes is also carried by line style, marker shape, or the legend text, so the chart remains fully legible if color is removed entirely (e.g. printed in black and white, or viewed by a colorblind user).

The axes labels can be formatted via the `axisLabel.formatter` option. You can customize the formatting to display the labels in a way that best suits your data and visualization needs. We provide predefined formatting functions like `unitFormatter`, `numberFormatter` and `numberShorthandFormatter`.

The default behavior of ECharts for justifiying axes labels is to avoid overlapping.This default behavior can hide more labels than necessary even when some space is still available. If you want labels to be placed more greedily, use `axisLabel.interval = 0` together with `hideOverlap: true`. This distributes the available space greedily from left to right on horizontal axes and from top to bottom on vertical axes. If a label does not fit into its slot, the space is released for the next tick, and labels are rendered either completely or not at all. This does only work for axis of type `category`.

When all axis labels should remain visible and be distributed evenly along the axis, configure the labels to use a fixed amount of space per tick. If the available space becomes insufficient, labels are automatically truncated. This behavior can be achieved with `axisLabel.interval = 0`, `axisLabel.width` (calculated based on the available space per tick), and `axisLabel.overflow = 'truncate'`. To keep the layout responsive, recalculate the label width on window resize and update the chart configuration accordingly. This does only work for axis of type `category`.

The legend provides a clear overview of all data series displayed in the chart. Each item reflects the series’ label, color, and visual style, ensuring users can quickly understand how values are grouped and represented. 

Depending on the selected chart type, the legend adapts its appearance. Line charts display a small line preview showing the stroke style, while bar charts use a solid color swatch that matches the bar fill. This makes it easy to distinguish series at a glance, regardless of the visualization style.
The default position of the legend is top. The legend can be positioned at the top of the chart by using the handle method `legendShow()` or `legendShow({ position: 'top' })`.
The legend can be positioned at the left of the chart by using the handle method `legendShow({ position: 'left' })`.
The legend can be positioned at the right of the chart by using the handle method `legendShow({ position: 'right' })`.
The legend can be positioned at the bottom of the chart by using the handle method `legendShow({ position: 'bottom' })`.

By default, the legend is interactive. Users can click on a legend item to toggle the visibility of the corresponding series in the chart. To make the legend non-interactive, use the *selectedMode: false* option.
The default story demonstrates a basic line chart configuration. The chart is configured via the `config` property, which accepts an object that maps directly to the ECharts option configuration.

The `config` property is the main way to configure the chart. It accepts an object that maps 1:1 to the ECharts option configuration. Assigning a new object to this property will update the chart with the new configuration.

Use the `palette` attribute to apply a Synergy design token color palette to chart series. `categorical` (12 distinct colors for comparing unrelated data series), `sequential-01`–`sequential-07` (10-step single-hue ramps), and `sequential-status-critical/error/info/success/warning` (10-step status ramps). If `option.color` is explicitly set, it takes precedence over the `palette` attribute.

Use `getInstance()` to access the underlying ECharts instance directly and work with its full native API. This is useful when the `config` property alone is not sufficient — for example to listen to ECharts events, trigger actions, or call `setOption()` with custom merge behavior. This example attaches a click listener via the native ECharts API. Click any data point to see the event payload logged to the browser console.

You can use multiple charts in one `<syn-chart>` instance, each with its own configuration. The palette colors or the default colors can be overridden per series item using the `color` property directly on the series object — allowing fine-grained control over individual chart series colors.

**Important:** The `color` property does **not** support CSS variables (e.g. `var(--syn-sequential-05-80)`). This is a limitation of ECharts itself: ECharts renders via the Canvas API, which does not resolve CSS custom properties. To use Synergy design tokens as colors, read the computed hex value first using `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--your-token').trim()` and pass the resolved value instead.

Line charts offer a clear way to visualize trends, changes and directional movements over time or across categories. By connecting individual data points, they highlight patterns such as growth, decline or stability at a glance, making them ideal for dashboards, KPI overviews and lightweight data summaries. 

The component provides flexible styling options that adapt to different visual needs, from straight linear segments to smooth curved lines. Combined with optional symbols, line charts can be tailored to emphasize exactly the level of detail or simplicity required in your layout.
The line chart can be configured with the `seriesLine` preset function.
The lines of line series can be hidden. When hidden, only the symbols remain, which is useful for minimal or simplified data displays.

The line series supports a variety of styles, including line width and line type (solid, dashed, dotted). When combining multiple line charts, ensure there’s sufficient visual differentiation, for example, by using distinct line styles.
The line series supports a variety of symbols.
The line series supports curved lines. Use the `smooth` property to enable smooth curves for the line series.
The line widths and symbol sizes can be adjusted to the needs.
The colors of the lines and symbols can be customized.

The tooltip provides contextual information when users hover or focus on data points within a chart. It displays values, labels without obstructing the view of the visualization. Use the `tooltipShow` preset to enable the tooltip.
Line charts can display both positive and negative values.

title.value: Line Chart with Positive and Negative Values

description.value: Zooming and panning allow users to focus on specific areas of a chart, especially when dealing with large datasets or dense series. The `dataZoom` option provides two types of zooming: integrated zooming and slider zooming. Integrated zooming enables direct interaction within the plotting area, while slider zooming allows users to define a specific data zoom level using handles and a selection bar.

When having large data sets or dense series where users need to inspect local trends without leaving the chart context, the `dataZoom` option with `type: 'inside'` can be used. It enables direct interaction inside the plotting area: 

- mouse drag to pan

- mouse wheel to zoom

 There are possibilities to customize the zooming behavior, for example, to restrict zooming to a specific axis, to set minimum and maximum zoom levels or to add an additional key for zooming. For more information have a look at the [ECharts documentation](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#dataZoom-inside)

The data zoom slider (the `dataZoom` option with `type: 'inside'`) allows users to define a specific data zoom level within a chart by dragging the left and right handles or moving the entire selection bar. It's commonly used in dashboards and analytics tools to filter, zoom, or focus on a subset of data without losing context of the full dataset. The component consists of three interactive elements: 

- Left handle: Defines the start of the selected zoom

- Right handle: Defines the end of the selected zoom

- Selection bar (center): Moves the entire zoom without changing its width

The slider can be customized in terms of position, size and appearance. For more information have a look at the [ECharts documentation](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#dataZoom-slider)

The donut chart component communicates the proportion of values within a one-dimensional data set using a ring made of evenly distributed, segmented arcs. Each segment size is normalized to 360 degrees based on its share of the total. A static, neutral inner ring frames the dynamic outer data ring.
The donut chart can either be configured via config with `type: 'synDonut'` or with the `seriesDonut` preset function.

By default, each outer ring segment is assigned a color from the chart's categorical color palette. Use the `colors` option to provide explicit colors instead; colors are repeated cyclically when fewer colors than data points are provided.

Use the `label` option to render a label for each segment, aligned by index with `data`. Each label is centered on its segment and placed outside the outer ring; provide a `prefixIcon` data URL alongside the `label` to render an icon before the label.
Use `legendShow()` to render legend entries for the donut segments. Segment names are used as legend labels and can be toggled interactively. For this use the `name` option in the data items.
Use the `center` option to position the donut inside the available layout area. Values can be pixels or percentages.

Use the `radius` option to define the donut's outer radius. The value can be specified either as a number (for a fixed pixel value, e.g. 20) or as a percentage string (e.g. '50%'). Percentage-based values automatically scale with the available space, while pixel values remain fixed.
Use `top`, `right`, `bottom`, and `left` to reduce the donut layout area from each side before `center` and `radius` are resolved. Insets can be set in pixels (number) or percentages (string).
Use status colors to visualize the distribution of items across different statuses, such as error, warning, success, and neutral.

Use the `label` property in the data items to apply custom label formatting. This can be a string or a function that receives the segment value and returns a formatted label. If the `label` is not set, the value will be used as the label. To omit the label completely, set the `label` to `undefined`.

The gauge chart component communicates a single value within a defined range using a semi-circular dial. The colored arc highlights status trends (e.g., safe / warning / critical), while the neutral track indicates the remaining capacity.
The gauge chart can either be configured via config with `type: 'synGauge'` or with the `seriesGauge` preset function.

The gauge series supports showing an outer sections ring. Use `sections.show: true` together with `sections.boundaries` or `sections.colors` to render a color-coded outer ring around the gauge, where each adjacent pair of boundary values defines a segment. When no `progressColor` is set, the progress arc automatically adopts the color of the segment containing the current value.

Use `trend.show: true` together with `trend.value` to render a small pill trend indicator above the gauge value; set `trend.direction` to `'up'` (default) or `'down'` to control the directional icon, and optionally provide `trend.iconUp` or `trend.iconDown` with a custom data URL to replace the default icons.
Use the `icon` option to render an SVG image below the unit label, or below the value when no unit is set.
The gauge series supports custom value formatting using `formatter.value`, `formatter.min`, and `formatter.max` options.

Segment charts visualize how values contribute to a whole by dividing data into proportional slices. They are well-suited for showing distribution, share ratios, or simple comparisons within a limited number of categories. You can choose between versions with or without gaps.
The segment chart can be configured via the chart config with `type: 'synSegment'` or with the `seriesSegment` preset function.

The `name` option sets the name of the segment chart, which is displayed in the gap of the chart when provided. The text styling can be overwritten via `nameTextStyle`. It can be used to e.g. change the appearance like color, overflow handling, positioning and other text-related properties.

By default, each segment item is assigned a color from the chart's categorical color palette. Use the `colors` option to provide explicit colors instead; colors are repeated cyclically when fewer colors than data points are provided.
Use `top`, `right`, `bottom`, and `left` to reduce the segment layout area from each side before segment rendering is done. Insets can be set in pixels (number) or percentages (string).

Use the `gap` option to set the size of the open section in the segment ring. It is defined as a fraction of the full circle (0–1) and defaults to `0.3`. Use `gapOrientation` to rotate the opening around the chart. By default, it is centered at the bottom.
Set `gap` to `0` to render no gap between the segments. Additionally a custom icon can be added to the inner circle via `icon` option.
Use the `min` and `max` options to define the value range for the segment chart. This is useful when values share a known scale, such as a range from 0 to 1.
Segment labels can be provided as strings or formatter functions. If no label is provided, the value is used by default; set `label` to `undefined` to omit a label.
Use the `weight` option on data items to control the relative width of each segment independently of its value. Segments without an explicit weight use the default weight.

Customize individual segments with `itemStyle`, `backgroundStyle` and `labelTextStyle`. Both `backgroundStyle` and `itemStyle` can be either set on chart or on data item level, `labelTextStyle` can only be set to the data item level. The chart level styling is inherited by all segments, while on the data item level it overrides the chart level styling for that specific segment.
Use `legendShow()` to display a legend for segment data items. Set the `name` option on each item to provide its legend label.

Place categories on the y-axis and values on the x-axis, where bar length represents value magnitude. Horizontal bar charts are best suited for:

- **Long category labels:** Provides ample horizontal room for text, avoiding overlapping, truncation, or awkward label rotations.
- **Large datasets:** Scales cleanly for 10 or more categories without compressing bar widths.
- **Rankings:** Naturally presents ordered lists (ascending or descending) in a top-to-bottom reading flow.

Place categories on the x-axis and values on the y-axis, where bar height represents value magnitude. Vertical bar charts work well for chronological trends and smaller category sets, and make differences in magnitude easy to compare.

Use `min` and `max` on the value axis to set explicit scale boundaries. Fixed ranges help standardize comparisons across charts, anchor benchmarks such as 0–100%, provide headroom for labels and tooltips, and prevent scale shifts when data changes.

Use `min` and `max` on the value axis to set explicit scale boundaries. Fixed ranges help standardize comparisons across charts, anchor benchmarks such as 0–100%, provide headroom for labels and tooltips, and prevent scale shifts when data changes. For stacked bar charts, account for the combined totals of the stacked series in each category so the full stacks fit within the scale.
Bar charts can show negative values such as deficits, losses, or decreases. Bars extend away from the zero baseline.

Bar charts can show negative values such as deficits, losses, or decreases. Bars extend away from the zero baseline. In stacked bar charts, negative values stack together below the zero baseline, separately from positive values.

title.value: Stacked Bar Charts with Negative Values

description.value: Bar charts can combine positive and negative values to show gains and losses or deviations from a baseline. Bars extend in opposite directions from zero.

title.value: Bar Charts with Positive and Negative Values

description.value: Bar charts can combine positive and negative values to show gains and losses or deviations from a baseline. Bars extend in opposite directions from zero. In stacked bar charts, positive and negative values accumulate separately on their respective sides of the zero baseline.

title.value: Stacked Bar Charts with Positive and Negative Values

description.value: Selection is disabled by default. Set `selectedMode` to `true` or `'single'` to select one data item at a time, `'multiple'` to select multiple data items, or `'series'` to select an entire series.

Enable a tooltip to inspect bar values on hover. For bar series it is recommended to set `tooltip.axisPointer.type` to `'shadow'` to highlight the corresponding category and compare its values across series.
Depending on your use case, choose a categorical palette (up to 12 colors) or a sequential palette (recommended for up to 3 colors).
Bar series use the chart's categorical palette by default. Use the `color` option to apply explicit colors to individual series.

Set `barWidth` to control bar thickness. A number specifies a fixed width in pixels, while a percentage string sets the width relative to the available category space and adapts to the chart size. By default, bars are responsive but capped at 24 px by the theme's `barMaxWidth` setting. To use bars wider than 24 px, also increase `barMaxWidth` on the series.
Use `legendShow()` to display a legend for named series. Series names become the legend labels, and users can toggle series visibility interactively.

Grouped bar charts display multiple bars per category to compare values across different series or subgroups. Choosing between a vertical (column) or horizontal orientation depends on the dataset and visualization goals.

A grouped bar chart is created when multiple bar series share the same category axis. The value axis defines the scale for the bar values. The bar chart can be configured via the chart config with `type: bar` or with the `seriesBar` preset function.

Single bar charts display one bar per category to compare discrete values or highlight a specific metric. Choosing between a vertical (column) or horizontal orientation depends on the dataset and visualization goals.
The bar chart can be configured via the chart config with `type: bar` or with the `seriesBar` preset function.

Set `large: true` to enable optimized rendering when a bar series contains many data points. The optimization is used once the number of items reaches `largeThreshold` (400 by default). Individual data-item styles cannot be customized while large rendering is active, so use it when rendering performance matters more than per-item styling.

title.value: Bar Chart with Large Data Set

description.value: Stacked bar charts display multiple series layered within a single bar per category. They are ideal for showing total values across categories while simultaneously breaking down proportional contributions. Choosing between a vertical or horizontal orientation depends on the dataset and visualization goals.

Configure a stacked bar chart with `type: 'bar'` and a shared `stack` identifier or use the `seriesBarStacked` preset function. Showing labels is recommended and their color should inherit the series color. Place labels to the left for vertical bars and above for horizontal bars. A 1 px border is recommended to better distinguish adjacent bar segments. The `seriesBarStacked` preset applies these label and border settings by default. It also sets `barCategoryGap` to control the spacing between category groups and `barMinWidth` to keep bars from becoming too narrow. These defaults help maintain readability, but cannot compensate for too little chart space or long value labels.

Area charts visualize trends while also highlighting the filled area beneath the line, making changes in magnitude easier to perceive. They are well‑suited for showing overall development, cumulative values, or comparing volumes over time.

An area chart can be configured via the chart config with `type: 'line'` and `areaStyle: {}` or with the `seriesArea` preset function. When using a config object, set `areaStyle.opacity` to `0.2` for the recommended styling. The `seriesArea` preset applies this opacity by default. Pass a custom `areaStyle` to override the preset default.
The area series supports curved lines. Use the `smooth` property to enable smooth curves.
The lines of area series can be hidden. When hidden, only the filled area remains for a more minimal, volume-focused visualization.
The line styles can be adjusted such as solid, dashed, and dotted as well as custom line widths. Use distinct styles to differentiate series when needed.
The data points can be marked via symbols. Set `symbol` and `symbolSize` on each series to customize them.
Use the `palette` attribute to apply another Synergy chart color palette to the area series.

By default, each area series is assigned a color from the chart's categorical color palette. Use the colors option to provide explicit colors instead. Colors are repeated cyclically when fewer colors than data points are provided.
Area charts can display both positive and negative values, filling each data point relative to the configured area origin.

title.value: Area Chart with Positive and Negative Values

description.value:
Use the `areaStyle.origin` option to choose the baseline from which an area is filled. Valid values:

- `auto` fills the area between the axis line and the data (**default**).
- `start` fills between the minimum axis value and the data.
- `end` fills between the maximum axis value and the data.
- A number fills between that specified value and the data.

The `stack` value names a stack group. Area series with the same `stack` value on the same category axis are stacked on top of one another. Use `stackStrategy` to control how values are accumulated:

- `samesign` stacks a value only when it has the same sign as the current stack total (**default**)
- `all` stacks values regardless of whether they are positive or negative
- `positive` stacks only positive values
- `negative` stacks only negative values
Set `emphasis.focus` to `series` to highlight the hovered area series and de-emphasize the others.
Enable contextual data point details with the `tooltipShow()` preset. The tooltip displays labels and values as users interact with the chart.
Use `legendShow()` to display a legend for named series. Series names become the legend labels, and users can toggle series visibility interactively.
Configure `dataZoom` to let users focus on a subset of an area chart's data. The slider provides handles for selecting the visible range.

An area range chart displays the area between two values over time. It is ideal for showing variability, uncertainty or value ranges, such as temperature highs and lows, forecast bands or best- and worst-case scenarios.

Use the `seriesAreaRange` preset function to create area range charts. This preset accepts each data point as a pair of lower and upper values and automatically generates the boundary lines, filled area and tooltip configuration. Its optional second argument accepts line series options that are merged into both boundary series and can override their defaults.

Alternatively, an area range can be configured using two stacked line series. Both series must use the same stack and name value. The first series contains the lower bound values and has its tooltip disabled. The second series contains the difference between the upper and lower values (upper - lower) and defines an areaStyle to render the shaded range. To display the actual range in the tooltip, format the second series' tooltip value using the original lower and upper values rather than the calculated difference values.
Set `smooth: true` to curve the upper and lower boundaries of the range.
Set `lineStyle.width` to `0` and configure `symbol` to show data point markers. When lines are hidden, only the filled range and its markers remain for a more minimal, range-focused visualization.
Customize range boundary lines with solid, dashed or dotted styles, and adjust their width. Use distinct styles to differentiate multiple area range series

title.value: Area Range Line Styles and Widths

description.value: Use `symbol` and `symbolSize` to choose the marker shape and size for area range data points. Set `symbol` to `none` to hide the markers.
Set the chart's `palette` attribute to apply a Synergy chart color palette to area range series.

By default, each series is assigned a color from the chart's categorical color palette. Use the colors option to provide explicit colors instead. Colors are repeated cyclically when fewer colors than data points are provided.
Area ranges can cross zero and include both positive and negative values. The chart displays the full lower-to-upper interval for each category.

title.value: Area Range with Positive and Negative Values

description.value: Enable contextual values for area range data points with the `tooltipShow()` preset. Give each series a name to identify it in the tooltip.
Use `legendShow()` to display a legend for named area range series. Users can select legend entries to toggle the corresponding ranges.

A mark line highlights a specific value in a chart, such as a target, maximum, minimum or average. Configure `markLine` on a specific series, the reference line is associated with that series and its data. It draws a horizontal or vertical line and can display a label with the value, providing immediate context without requiring users to read exact axis values. By default, the line uses a neutral color so it adds context without competing with the data series.

For the full configuration possibilities have a look at [ECharts documentation](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#series-line.markLine)
Use `type: 'min'` and `type: 'max'` in `markLine.data` to highlight the minimum and maximum values of a series.
Use `type: 'average'` in `markLine.data` to show the average value of a series as a reference line.
Add a `yAxis` value to `markLine.data` to draw a horizontal threshold line. Use an `xAxis` value for a vertical line at a specific category.
Define a mark line with a pair of `coord` points to connect custom coordinates. Configure `symbol` to control the symbols at either end of the line.

Use Synergy's NAMUR status colors when a reference line needs to communicate intent: green for a target that has been met, red for an exceeded limit or critical threshold and yellow/orange for a warning.

The label position can be configured using `label.position`. While several positions are supported, `start` and `end` are generally recommended. To ensure long labels remain fully visible, adjust the chart grid (for example `grid.left`, `grid.top`, etc.) to provide sufficient space around the chart area. 
Use `label.formatter` to customize the displayed text, such as combining the mark line name with the value.
Hide the label for a mark line by setting `label.show` to `false`.

A mark area highlights a range along an axis, such as a target interval, threshold, or time window. It is rendered behind the data to provide context without adding another series. Use a low-contrast fill or pattern so the data remains easy to read, and add a descriptive label to each range so its meaning does not rely on color or pattern alone. Configure `markArea` on a series and define each range with a pair of points.

For the full configuration possibilities, see the [ECharts documentation](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#series-line.markArea).
Use predefined types like `average`, `min` or `max` as start or endpoints in `markArea.data.type`.
Add `yAxis` values to the two points in `markArea.data` to highlight a horizontal value range across the chart. The area spans the full category axis between the specified values.
Add `xAxis` category values to the two points in `markArea.data` to highlight a range of categories. You can define multiple areas to call out separate periods and give each area a name for context.

The label position can be configured using `label.position`. While multiple positions are supported, 'insideLeft' is recommended for horizontal mark areas and 'insideTop' for vertical mark areas. The default position is 'insideLeft'.

Use Synergy's NAMUR status colors when a highlighted range needs to communicate intent: green for a target that has been met, red for an exceeded limit or critical range, and yellow/orange for a warning. Set the area color in `itemStyle` and use opacity to keep the data visible beneath it.

A mark point highlights an individual location in a series, such as an extreme value, an inspection or a significant event. Configure `markPoint` on the associated series and define its markers in `markPoint.data`. By default, markers use a compact neutral pin with a value label inside it.

For the full configuration possibilities, see the [ECharts documentation](https://echarts.apache.org/en/option.html#series-line.markPoint).
Use predefined types like `average`, `min` or `max` as points in `markPoint.data.type`.

Set `coord: [category, value]` on each marker to highlight specific data coordinates. Use `name` for descriptive context and `value` for the value exposed to label formatters. Coordinates may also use numeric values on value axes.

Configure `symbol` and `symbolSize` on `markPoint` for all markers or on individual data entries to override them. Built-in shapes include `circle`, `diamond`, and `triangle`. Keep markers compact so they do not obscure the data, and pair shapes with descriptive labels.

Customize individual mark points with `symbol`, `symbolSize`, `label.position` and `itemStyle.color`. Pair color with distinct shapes and meaningful labels so status remains clear without relying on color alone.

By default, mark points use pin-shaped markers with the value shown inside. When a descriptive label is too long to fit in the pin, use a compact symbol such as `circle` and position the label outside of it.

A histogram visualizes the frequency distribution of numerical values across continuous intervals (bins). It helps identify patterns, spread, clusters and outliers within a dataset. Histograms are best suited for analyzing distributions of continuous data, such as response times, measurements and durations. Histogram bins follow a meaningful numerical order and should not be reordered. If values represent distinct categories that should be reordered or compared independently, use a bar chart instead.

Configure a histogram with a series of `type: 'bar'` and set `barMaxWidth` to `'100%'` to let bars fill the available category space or use the `seriesHistogram` preset for the recommended configuration.

A vertical histogram displays value intervals along the x-axis and their frequencies along the y-axis. This orientation is commonly used when there is sufficient horizontal space and makes it easy to compare the distribution across value ranges.

A horizontal histogram displays value intervals along the y-axis and their frequencies along the x-axis. This orientation can improve readability when interval labels are long or when vertical space is more limited.

Use `min` and `max` on the value axis to set explicit scale boundaries. This ensures the axis scale remains consistent across datasets, making it easier to compare multiple charts and monitor changes over time.
A histogram can show negative values such as losses, deficits or decreases. Bars extend below the zero baseline to represent the frequency of values within negative ranges.

A histogram can be used to visualize the distribution of positive and negative changes around a reference value. Negative bars represent decreases or values below the reference, while positive bars indicate increases or values above it.

title.value: Histogram with Positive and Negative Values

description.value: Set `barWidth` to control bar thickness. A number specifies a fixed width in pixels, while a percentage string sets the width relative to the available category space and adapts to the chart size. Histograms are typically displayed with little or no gap between bars to emphasize the continuity of the underlying distribution. When `barWidth` is set, `barCategoryGap` is ignored.
Set `barCategoryGap` to `0` to remove the gap between histogram bars, emphasizing the continuity of the distribution.
Bar series use the chart's categorical palette by default. Use the `color` option to apply explicit colors to individual series.

Enable a tooltip to inspect bar values on hover. For bar series it is recommended to set `tooltip.axisPointer.type` to `'shadow'` to highlight the corresponding category and compare its values across series.

A histogram summarizes large datasets by grouping values into bins. In image processing, the bins can represent grayscale intensities from 0 (black) to 255 (white), and each bar shows the number of pixels at that intensity.

Bullet charts provide a compact comparison of a measured value with a reference range. Use them to monitor operating conditions, production metrics or other KPIs against their expected limits. In this implementation, the bar shows the range and the contrasting marker shows the actual value. Label the metric and its units, and provide a text alternative or data table.

Configure a bullet chart via the chart config with `type: 'synBullet'` or with the `seriesBullet` preset function. Each data item requires numeric `start`, `end` and `current` values: the range extends from `start` to `end` and the marker shows `current`, which can be inside or outside the range. Range thickness adapts to the available category space and is capped by `barMaxWidth` by default.
Place categories on the x-axis and values on the y-axis to compare actual values with their reference ranges vertically. This orientation works well for a small number of categories.
Place categories on the y-axis and values on the x-axis. Horizontal bullets provide more room for category labels and can be useful for compact KPI dashboards.
Use `colorBy: 'data'` to assign range colors by item or `colorBy: 'series'` to give the items in a series the same color.
Use the `palette` attribute to apply another Synergy chart color palette to the bullet series.
Set `itemStyle` on the series or on individual data items to customize range colors, border or shadows. Use Synergy chart tokens and keep the actual-value marker distinguishable from the range.

Enable a tooltip to inspect the range and actual value on hover. Set a `name` on each data item to show it in the tooltip. Without a name, the category label is used instead. Set `tooltip.axisPointer.type` to `'shadow'` to highlight the corresponding category and compare values across series.
Show a legend for named bullet items so users can identify ranges and toggle individual items.
Set `min` and `max` on the value axis to keep the scale consistent across charts or updates. Include the relevant range endpoints and actual values so they remain visible.

Set `barWidth` to control the thickness of the bullet range. A number specifies a fixed width in pixels, while a percentage string sets the width relative to the category band and adapts to the chart size. By default, ranges are responsive but capped at 24 px by the theme's `barMaxWidth` setting. To use ranges wider than 24 px, increase `barMaxWidth` on the series or explicitly set `barMaxWidth: undefined` in the initial series configuration to remove the maximum. Explicit `barWidth` ignores `barCategoryGap` and remains subject to `barMinWidth`.

Use `markerStyle` to set the actual-value marker's color, border, opacity, width and height. Width and height are physical pixel dimensions independent of orientation; the marker remains centered on the actual value.

accessibility: Do not rely on color alone to distinguish data series; use labels, markers, or patterns where helpful.
Provide a text alternative or data table for users who cannot interpret visualizations reliably.
Ensure chart context is available in surrounding text, including what is shown and why it matters.

content: Use charts when visual pattern recognition (trends, peaks, outliers) is more helpful than raw tables.
Keep the chart goal specific and clear (for example trend over time, comparison, distribution).
Avoid using charts when exact value lookup is the primary task; provide a table or value list as a complement.
usageGuidelines.name: Data and Purpose

content: Use line charts for trends across ordered data, such as time or sequence; avoid connecting categories that have no meaningful order.
Use area charts to emphasize magnitude across an ordered sequence. Prefer lines when overlapping filled areas would obscure comparisons.
Use area-range charts to show lower and upper bounds, such as a minimum-to-maximum range or uncertainty band.
Use bars to compare discrete categories; group bars for side-by-side series comparisons and stack them when each category total and its parts are meaningful.
Use histograms to show the distribution of a continuous measure grouped into value intervals, not to compare unrelated categories.
Use a donut chart to show a small number of categories as proportions of one whole; use bars or a table when precise comparisons between values matter.
Use a gauge for one current value against a defined scale or thresholds, rather than to show a time trend.
Use a bullet chart to compare an actual value with its displayed range, such as a target or acceptable range.
Use a segment chart for several independent radial progress indicators; do not imply that the segments are parts of one whole.
usageGuidelines.name: Choosing a Chart Type

content: Use clear axis labels, units, and legends so users can understand the data context immediately.
Limit the number of simultaneously visible series to reduce visual noise.
Choose palettes that maintain sufficient contrast between series and background.
Avoid excessive decoration and effects that do not add analytical value.
usageGuidelines.name: Visual Clarity

content: Ensure labels, tooltips, and legends remain readable at small viewport sizes.
Prevent overlapping labels and crowded markers by simplifying or reducing displayed data where needed.
Keep chart dimensions appropriate for the amount and complexity of the data shown.
usageGuidelines.name: Responsiveness and Density

useCases: Display time-based trends such as sensor values, throughput, or production metrics.
Compare multiple data series in dashboards to identify differences and anomalies.
Present historical data to support analysis, reporting, and decision-making.
Visualize key performance indicators where users need a fast visual overview.

custom.summary: The `<syn-chart>` component is a container for displaying charts. It provides a structured layout and styling for chart elements, allowing for consistent presentation across different types of charts. The chart component is based on [Apache ECharts](https://echarts.apache.org)
